author: reek
body: A software-rendered 3D scene running in the desktop's content pane, on whatever framebuffer the firmware handed us. No host rasterizer and no GPU: every triangle is projected, shaded and filled by Renderer3D, and every pixel is a poke-32 into the panel.

author: reek
body: It draws into the content rectangle rather than the whole panel, so the sidebar, the top bar, the taskbar and the running clock stay on the glass around a moving view.

author: reek
body: The scene is rendered into a back buffer and blitted to the pane in one pass rather than rasterized straight at the framebuffer. Painting in place is visible while it happens: the clear lands first, so a viewer sees the pane flash to sky and refill on every frame, and a capture taken mid-frame shows only the nodes drawn by then. The blit costs one read and one write per pixel of the pane against the clear's one write, and that is what the steady picture is bought with.

author: reek
body: The target is built once. Rebuilding it would allocate a fresh colour and depth buffer every frame, and at this size that is megabytes a frame that never come back.

author: reek
body: The camera orbits on the PIT tick, so the rotation runs at wall-clock speed whatever the frame rate. The angle goes through Cordic rather than Matrix4's mat4-sin-approx: that one is a two-term Taylor valid only near zero, and at half a turn it answers -2.03 where the sine is 0. Cordic quadrant-reduces and is honest all the way round.

author: reek
body: Built once. Only the camera changes per frame, through a record copy that leaves the meshes alone -- rebuilding the scene would rebuild every vertex and index list in it.

author: reek
body: The blit is the one step that has to know both pitches: the pane's rows sit stride apart on the panel and w apart in the back buffer.

author: reek
body: One frame: clear the back buffer, point the camera, render, blit to the pane, then the hint line. The hint goes onto the panel after the blit because the blit covers it.

author: reek
body: Esc leaves. The self tail call keeps the loop constant-stack, and the angle is derived from the tick counter rather than accumulated, so a slow frame loses no rotation and a fast one gains none.

author: reek
body: The cursor is hidden for the whole run rather than saved under each frame: the view repaints continuously, so a save-under patch would be stale the instant it was taken and the first restore would stamp a ghost onto the scene.

author: val
body: Cordic answers on a scale of 1000 and takes milliradians, 6283 to the turn. The orbit radius is 5200 world units, so the scaled cosine is multiplied by 5.2.

author: val
body: The software pass builds its map in Codex a triangle at a time, so it stays at 256; the map is rebuilt every frame inside the frame's bracket, so its half megabyte is reclaimed with the frame.

author: val
body: The host rasterizer fills its map in C and can afford 1024. The map covers the whole scene and the ground is 3000 units across, so at 256 a texel lands on many screen pixels and every shadow edge shows texel-shaped teeth.

author: val
body: `kbd-pump-one` advances a three-phase state machine (arm, check, drain) one step per call, and a software frame costs about a second on metal, so one poll per frame is a report every three seconds. Measured on the ASUS 2026-08-08: keys were swallowed unless held and Esc did not close the pane. Polling until the machine yields costs microseconds against the frame.

author: val
body: Milliradians of yaw per device pixel; `gsc-turn` is 6283, so a full turn is 785 pixels of travel at 8. The delta is clamped BEFORE use because an unclamped jump plus one `gsc-turn` can land negative, and `int-mod` of a negative is not a wrap.

author: val
body: The buffers are sized from the content box at open and the box changes while the pane is up: docking the task band to a vertical edge at 1600x900 grows it from 1,280,000 to 1,321,664 words, 166 KB past both buffers per frame (measured 2026-09-07, `desk-cbox-drift`). `r3d-base-ok` sees the base, not the extent, so the target is clamped here.

author: val
body: The orbit runs off the HPET counter because the RTC's one-second granularity rendered 43 identical frames and then jumped six degrees. The counter is HALTED until the enable bit is set, and a halted counter reads a constant that looks like a stopped animation, so `hpet-start` runs here (two MMIO reads when already set). It is read, never waited on, so the ASUS losing its timer INTERRUPT about 54 s after boot does not reach it; a board with no HPET answers zero and falls back to the RTC.

author: val
body: The host rasterizer clears its whole viewport and draws far faster than the glass is sampled, so a label inside the viewport reads as absent about as often as present. The view stops 20 rows short of the label.

author: val
body: The ground texture uploads once, at open. Each commit costs a host-side allocation, a copy out of guest RAM and a host diagnostic line: driven per frame it fired 301 times in nine seconds and cut the interactive pane to about a frame a second.

author: val
body: A software frame costs about a second on metal, so a repaint that is not a new frame blits the target the last frame left. The host rasterizer keeps no copy in guest memory and renders one bracketed frame instead.
